(Joao Paulo Burini/Getty Images) (NEW YORK) — The Florida Department of Health confirmed the state’s first death from dengue fever this year as cases of the mosquito-borne illness continue to rise. The department did not provide any details about the patient including name, age, sex or residence. The Tampa Bay Times, which first reported the death, described the patient as an 80-year-old Tampa woman who died on Sept. 4. The FDOH did not immediately return ABC News’ request for comment. For the week ending Sept. 12, Florida has confirmed 152 locally acquired cases of dengue, according to data from the state health department. This is the highest number recorded since 2023, when the state saw 189 locally acquired cases over the course of the year, data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows. Hillsborough County — which includes Tampa — has reported the most cases so far this year with 134, according to the FDOH. Other counties with confirmed cases include Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco and Pinellas. Dengue viruses are spread through bites from infected Aedes species mosquitoes, mostly found in tropical and subtropical regions, according to the CDC. These mosquitoes are also responsible for spreading Zika and chikungunya viruses. Dengue can be caused by dengue virus strains 1, 2, 3 or 4. A person also can be infected with dengue multiple times over the course of their life. About one in four people who contract dengue develop symptoms which typically last two to seven days and are usually mild. This may include fever, rash, nausea, vomiting, muscle pain, joint pain and bone pain. About one in 20 infected people will develop severe dengue, which can lead to shock, internal bleeding and, in some cases, death, the CDC said. There are no disease-specific treatments for dengue. The CDC recommends rest, fluids and over-the-counter medications to relieve symptoms. Patients with severe illness often need to be hospitalized and receive additional supportive treatments, such as intravenous fluids. The CDC warns patients not to take aspirin or ibuprofen; it can trigger inflammation or bleeding of the stomach lining. Currently, there is no dengue vaccine available in the U.S. In 2021, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a vaccine for children between ages 9 and 16 who have a laboratory-confirmed previous dengue virus infection and live in areas where dengue is endemic, but it has since been discontinued. Methods to help prevent dengue infection include using effective mosquito repellents, wearing long-sleeve shirts and long pants when outside and staying in places with air conditioning when possible. The CDC also recommends emptying containers of still or stagnant water to eliminate places where mosquitos can breed. ABC News’ Youri Benadjaoud contributed to this report. Under the agreement announced on Friday, September 18, 2026, the Hyderabad-based pharmaceutical company will handle the private distribution of the Qdenga vaccine for both paediatric and adult populations. The vaccine, which received marketing authorisation from India's Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) in July 2026, is projected to become available in the first half of 2027. The collaboration represents a significant commercial and public health development in a country that has experienced an 11-fold increase in reported dengue cases over the past two decades. Financial terms of the distribution agreement remain confidential, but Takeda will retain full legal ownership of the vaccine, control over its manufacturing, and commercialisation rights for India's public procurement market. By securing exclusive private distribution rights, Dr. Reddy's bypasses standard price-capped therapeutic segments, capturing high-barrier retail vaccination flows in India's expanding urban healthcare markets. This move aligns with the company's broader strategy to pivot toward speciality pharmaceutical assets, complementing its existing portfolio of generic medicines. Following the announcement, shares of Dr. Reddy's Laboratories rose by up to 3 percent on the Bombay Stock Exchange, reaching an intraday high of ₹1,207.50. Regulatory Approval and Vaccine Mechanics The CDSCO cleared Qdenga—technically known as TAK-003—for individuals aged 4 to 60 years. Developed using recombinant DNA technology, the live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine is designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes. Scientists built the vaccine on a weakened dengue virus type-2 (DENV-2) backbone, engineering it to include structural surface proteins from the DENV-1, DENV-3, and DENV-4 strains. This structural approach aims to provide broad immune coverage regardless of which specific serotype a patient encounters in the environment. Healthcare providers will administer the vaccine through subcutaneous injection in a two-dose regimen, spaced three months apart. Crucially, the World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended Qdenga for use in highly endemic countries without requiring pre-vaccination screening for prior dengue exposure. The absence of a pre-vaccination testing requirement streamlines administration in busy clinical settings, avoiding the delays and costs associated with serological screening. India's Dengue Burden and Serotype Circulation The introduction of a tetravalent vaccine addresses a complex epidemiological challenge in India. Dengue is an endemic mosquito-borne viral infection that causes severe flu-like illness, and in extreme cases, can progress to severe dengue accompanied by bleeding, organ impairment, and plasma leakage. Urbanisation, changing climate patterns, and increased domestic travel have expanded the geographical footprint of the Aedes aegypti mosquito, the primary vector for the virus. Consequently, hospitals routinely face severe capacity constraints during the peak monsoon and post-monsoon transmission seasons. A recent nationwide molecular surveillance study conducted by the Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratory of the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) illustrated the complexity of the local outbreak environment. The research confirmed that all four dengue serotypes are currently co-circulating across multiple regions of the country. Furthermore, the study found that one in 14 patients carried concurrent infections with multiple dengue serotypes. Because infection with one serotype does not confer long-term immunity against the others—and subsequent infections with different serotypes carry a higher risk of severe disease—a vaccine that addresses all four strains simultaneously is considered essential for effective population-level protection. Clinical Efficacy and Global Precedent Takeda has gathered substantial clinical data supporting the vaccine's efficacy through an extensive global clinical development programme involving more than 60,000 participants across endemic and non-endemic regions. According to a 2025 analysis released by Takeda, clinical trials demonstrated a 61.2 percent overall efficacy rate against virologically confirmed dengue. More importantly for public health systems, the vaccine showed an 84.1 percent efficacy rate in preventing dengue-related hospitalisations at a 4.5-year follow-up after vaccination. Since its initial regulatory clearances in 2022, Qdenga has secured approvals in more than 40 countries. The manufacturer reports that more than 32 million doses have already been distributed worldwide through various public and private immunisation programmes. The vaccine also holds a WHO prequalification, a designation that ensures the product meets stringent international standards for quality, safety, and efficacy. Public Health Integration and Future Milestones While the current agreement focuses exclusively on the private sector, both companies view the retail market launch as the first step in a broader deployment strategy. Regulatory processes, including price determination and the finalisation of local quality-assurance protocols, are ongoing. The precise pricing structure for the Indian market has not yet been announced, as the companies navigate the final administrative steps required before commercial distribution. Takeda executives have stated that securing a position in India's Universal Immunisation Programme remains a primary long-term objective. A recent recommendation by the Parliamentary Committee on Health to consider incorporating a dengue vaccine into the national programme suggests growing institutional support for public procurement. In the interim, Dr. Reddy's will leverage its extensive domestic distribution network to make the vaccine accessible to eligible patients who can afford private healthcare. The companies will jointly conduct disease awareness campaigns and engage with healthcare professionals to prepare for the 2027 rollout. Medical experts caution that while the vaccine provides a vital new tool, it must complement rather than replace existing vector control measures. Continued public health efforts to eliminate stagnant water and reduce mosquito populations remain necessary to comprehensively manage the disease burden in urban and rural communities alike. content: Homepage Latest News Cuba News Miami News Blackouts today Informal Exchange Rate Videos Entertainment Sports International News Opinion CiberCuba Interviews United States Cuisine Florida Spain Culture Motor Readings Tourism History Nature Health Close the sidebar ESENFRIT Dengue in Cuba exceeds 7.4 times the expected level for 2026, and the peak typically occurs in October Latest News By CiberCuba Editorial Team Tuesday, September 22, 2026 - 6:42 PM Mosquito Aedes aegyptiPhoto © isglobal.org Cuba has recorded 7,133 cases of dengue in 2026, a figure that greatly exceeds the usual levels for this time of year, according to updated data from the Global Dengue Observatory (GDO) at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine. The observatory, which uses official data and statistical models to estimate the progression of the disease, places the current season at elevated levels and calculates that the reported and estimated cases so far represent approximately 7.4 times the expected level based on the country's historical behavior. "As of 2026, the reported cases far exceed the anticipated figures. Currently, the cases are on the rise, as expected for this time of year according to trends from previous years," stated the GDO in its analysis. August recorded the highest increase August recorded the highest monthly figure in recent months, with an estimated 3,214 cases, a number "far higher than what would typically be expected at this time of year." In July, the estimate had been 2,173 cases. The GDO clarifies that the official available data extends up to June, while the subsequent figures correspond to estimates made to adjust for the usual delays in epidemiological reporting. The situation could worsen in the coming weeks. According to historical patterns of dengue in Cuba, October tends to be the month with the highest transmission activity, meaning the country may not have reached the peak of the season yet. Graph showing the evolution of dengue cases in Cuba in 2026. Screenshot/Global Dengue Observatory. Four serotypes of the virus circulate on the island The increase in cases comes after the Ministry of Public Health (MINSAP) warned in June about the risk of a dengue epidemic. The Deputy Minister of Public Health, Carilda Peña, then warned that all four serotypes of the virus are circulating simultaneously in Cuba: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4. The presence of multiple serotypes increases the risk of complications, especially in individuals who have previously suffered from dengue and may become infected with a different variant of the virus. The main sources of transmission are currently concentrated in Guantánamo, Villa Clara, and Matanzas. As of September 9, the municipalities of Imías, Baracoa, and Guantánamo city were experiencing active transmission, with more than 30 confirmed cases by PCR and circulation of serotypes 2, 3, and 4. This week, the Guantanamo municipality of Manuel Tames was declared in a state of alarm due to the increase in dengue cases. In Villa Clara, the municipality of Ranchuelo reported an increase in patients with hemorrhagic dengue, with at least 12 individuals hospitalized during the outbreak. Trash, standing water, and power outages favor the mosquito The expansion of dengue occurs in a context marked by issues that favor the reproduction of the Aedes aegypti mosquito, the main transmitter of the virus. The accumulation of garbage, water leaks, and the need to store it during power outages have been identified by specialists and health authorities as factors that complicate vector control. The current increase follows a 2025 marked by a strong circulation of arboviruses in Cuba. The MINSAP reported that that year more than 81,900 cases of dengue and chikungunya were recorded and acknowledged at least 55 fatalities. How dengue spreads The dengue virus does not spread from person to person through respiratory droplets. It is transmitted by infected mosquitoes, primarily the yellow fever mosquito, Aedes aegypti, which is widespread in Florida. They need only a small amount of standing water to breed and can bite throughout the day, not just at dawn or after sunset. A mosquito becomes infected after biting an infected person and can transmit the virus to someone else several days later. Approximately three-quarters of infected people develop no symptoms. In others, signs of illness usually appear 4–10 days after the bite. Dengue is also known as “breakbone fever” because of the severe pain it can cause in the muscles, joints, and bones. Typical symptoms include: a sudden high fever, severe headache and pain behind the eyes, nausea, vomiting, and a blotchy rash. There are four types of dengue virus. A previous infection usually provides long-lasting protection against only one of them. A second infection with a different type can increase the risk of severe illness. Why severe dengue is dangerous Most patients recover in about a week. However, approximately one in 20 patients develops severe dengue, often just as the fever begins to subside – on the third to seventh day of illness. Fluid leaking from small blood vessels can lead to a sharp drop in blood pressure, bleeding, and organ damage. Those at greatest risk include infants, pregnant women, people over 65, and patients with diabetes, obesity, or kidney disease. Warning signs include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool, and extreme drowsiness or restlessness. Without treatment, severe dengue can be fatal for approximately 10% of patients. With timely hospitalization, that figure falls to less than 1%. There is no specific antiviral drug for dengue, so treatment involves controlling the fever, restoring fluid levels, and monitoring the patient’s condition. Aspirin, ibuprofen, and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can increase the risk of bleeding. Dengue is spreading beyond the tropics According to the World Health Organization, more than 14 million cases of dengue were reported worldwide in 2024 across approximately 100 countries. That is a 2,600% increase from the more than 505,000 cases recorded in 2000. Rising temperatures, rapid urban growth, and international travel are contributing to the spread of the virus. In the United States, most cases are still linked to infections acquired abroad. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported nearly 1,900 such cases in 2023 alone. However, in warm states, infected travelers can initiate local chains of transmission because mosquito vectors already live there. Of the 50 U.S. states, Florida faces the highest risk. More than 300 locally acquired cases were reported in Miami-Dade County between 2010 and 2024. Local transmission has also been recorded in Texas, California, Arizona, and Hawaii. A dengue vaccine exists, but it is used only in certain situations, including for children who live in areas with high levels of virus transmission and have previously had dengue. Therefore, reducing the risk depends primarily on protecting against mosquito bites and seeking medical care promptly if symptoms appear. The Florida Department of Health confirmed on Sept. 18, 2026, that the death of an elderly woman on Sept. 4 was due to dengue fever. This is the first confirmed death in a larger dengue outbreak in Hillsborough County, which has seen 134 cases of the disease this summer. In August, the Hillsborough County Health Department issued a mosquito-borne illness alert due to reports of multiple locally acquired cases. This cluster of locally spread cases is a stark reminder that a disease which most Americans associate with faraway tropical vacations is increasingly being caught at home. Ad Feedback Dengue is often called “breakbone fever,” and the nickname is earned. People who get sick typically develop a sudden high fever along with a pounding headache, pain behind the eyes and deep aches in the muscles, joints and bones. Many also feel nauseated, throw up or break out in a blotchy rash a few days in. As an infectious diseases physician and tropical medicine specialist who directs a travel clinic, I see how easily dengue slips past both patients and doctors. In parts of the U.S. where the disease is still uncommon, it is easily mistaken for the flu or COVID-19, and that delay can be dangerous. Related article Northern house mosquito (Culex pipiens) with reflection on the blue water surface, macro shot with generous copy space, selected focus, narrow depth of field fermate/iStockphoto/Getty Images Mosquitoes bite! 5 tips for making yourself less attractive to them 5 min read How it spreads Dengue is not passed from person to person like a cold. It spreads through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes, mainly Aedes aegypti, a species commonly found in Florida. These mosquitoes thrive in warm cities and can breed in as little as a bottle capful of standing water. These mosquitoes bite during the day, not just at dusk. The cycle is simple and hard to break: A mosquito bites an infected person, then bites someone else days later, giving them the virus. Read more: We studied 3 Florida mosquito species to learn why they like some people more than others Dengue is especially tricky because most infections cause no symptoms at all. Roughly 3 in 4 people who catch the virus never feel sick. For the 25% who are symptomatic, those symptoms don’t appear until four to 10 days after being bitten. In addition, there are four different strains of the dengue virus, and surviving one gives you lasting protection against only that one. A second infection with a different type actually raises the odds of severe disease. A life-threatening turn Most people suffer with dengue for a miserable week and then recover on their own. But about 1 in 20 patients progress to severe dengue, a life-threatening turn that tends to strike just as the fever breaks – often around days three to seven, when patients and their families may wrongly assume the worst is over. In severe dengue, tiny blood vessels throughout the body start leaking fluid, blood pressure can crash and dangerous bleeding or organ damage can follow. Warning signs that someone is sliding into this phase include severe belly pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding from the gums or nose, extreme drowsiness or restlessness, and blood in vomit or stool. Some groups face higher risk, including infants, pregnant women, adults over 65 and people with conditions like diabetes, obesity or kidney disease. Left untreated, severe dengue can kill up to 10% of patients. With prompt hospital care, that number drops below 1 in 100 – which is why recognizing it early matters so much. A dengue vaccine exists, but it is not recommended for the average American traveler. The available shots are used only in select cases, such as children who live in high-transmission areas and have already had dengue once. So prevention still rests mostly on avoiding mosquito bites. Related article An adult female blacklegged tick (Ixodes scapularis) is shown questing on a stick, 2023. Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images The bugs are getting worse 11 min read How dengue is treated There is no antiviral drug that cures dengue. Care is all about supporting the body while it fights the virus. For people well enough to stay home, that means rest, plenty of fluids and acetaminophen, commonly known in the U.S. by the brand name Tylenol, for fever and pain. Patients who may have dengue must avoid aspirin, ibuprofen and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. These drugs raise the risk of bleeding, which is already a danger with dengue. Read more: Dengue fever is a growing problem: why it’s so hard to beat with vaccines Patients who develop more severe symptoms need to be admitted to the hospital, where doctors give carefully measured intravenous fluids and watch closely. Too little fluid and the patient can go into shock; too much and the lungs can flood. A worsening global problem Dengue is surging worldwide. The World Health Organization recorded more than 14 million cases in 2024, its worst year on record, across some 100 countries. That’s a 2,600% increase from the more than 505,000 cases reported in 2000. Warmer temperatures, rapid urban growth and global travel are all helping the mosquitoes – and the virus – expand into places where it has never been a problem before. South Asia, Southeast Asia and Latin America carry the heaviest burden, but the map is spreading north. Related article Michelle Mingrone checks on mosquito traps in her yard in the morning of Monday, June 15, 2026, in Washington, DC. /Maansi Srivastava Why can’t we just get rid of mosquitoes? One fed-up community is trying 7 min read Why the U.S. should pay attention Most U.S. dengue cases are still picked up abroad. Travelers return home sick. In 2023 alone, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported nearly 1,900 such travel-related cases. But every infected traveler is a spark, and in warm states the tinder is already there. In the U.S. territories, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands see the most cases by far. Florida has the highest risk among the 50 states, with Miami-Dade County recording more than 300 locally acquired dengue infections between 2010 and 2024. Local cases have also turned up in Texas, California, Arizona and Hawaii. Read more: How do mosquito repellents work? What to do if you think you have dengue If you develop a sudden fever after traveling to a dengue-prone area, or after mosquito exposure in South Florida, see a doctor and mention where you’ve been. Rest, drink fluids and use acetaminophen – not ibuprofen or aspirin. Most importantly, watch for the warning signs. Severe belly pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding or sudden drowsiness means get to an emergency room right away. And to protect yourself and your neighbors: Use insect repellent, wear long sleeves and dump out any standing water in your yard where mosquitoes breed. content: Two more locally aquired cases of dengue fever in Orange County have prompted county officials to step up efforts to fight the pesky insects and the Florida Department of Health to issue an alert about mosquito-borne diseases. The first advisory about dengue fever was issued Sept. 2 by state officials after a case was confirmed in Pine Hills. The additional cases announced Friday are in the Apopka area and prompted another state alert. The culprits are Aedes aegypti, primarily daytime biters that thrive in urban and suburban areas and breed in flowerpots, buckets and other smaller containers, said Steve Harrison, manager of Orange County Mosquito Control. “We have a robust population of those,” he said of the species, sometimes called yellow fever mosquitos. “If residents go out in their yards and find containers holding water, more than likely there will be Aedes aegypti larvae in them.” Empty them, he advised. If larvae are in the containers, adult mosquitoes are around the property, too, Harrison said. The mosquitoes are homebodies, typically flying no more than 200 yards from where they emerged as larvae. Florida leads the nation in dengue cases this year with 270 reported so far. Specialist Jenifer Gonzalez studies dead mosquitos to be tested for Dengue fever in the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Specialist Jonah Mock prepares samples to be tested for Dengue fever in the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Specialist Rafael Melendez, left, consults with lab manager Jose Colon while studying dead mosquitos to be tested for Dengue fever in the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Specialist Jonah Mock holds a sample to be tested for dengue fever in the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Specialists Rafael Melendez, right, and Jenifer Gonzalez study dead mosquitos to be tested for Dengue fever in the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Specialist Jonah Mock prepares samples to be tested for Dengue fever in the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Show Caption 1 of 6 Specialist Jenifer Gonzalez studies dead mosquitos to be tested for Dengue fever in the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Expand Mosquito-borne dengue fever is commonly found in tropical and subtropical regions. Typical symptoms are a high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle, bone or joint pain, nausea and vomiting, swollen glands, and skin rash. While many species of mosquito inhabit Florida, only two transmit dengue: Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. Recognizable by their dark bodies and distinct white-striped legs, these biters peak just after sunrise and before sunset. They also can transmit Zika, yellow fever, and chikungunya . Aedes aegypti are native to north Africa and considered an invasive species here. A species collection displays the Aedes aegypti mosquito that is responsible for the dengue fever being tested by the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Last month, the Florida Department of Health in Orange County advised residents of an increase in mosquito-borne disease activity in the area. Several sentinel chickens have tested positive for West Nile virus. Sentinel chickens are healthy birds placed in outdoor coops and monitored by public health departments in the hopes of detecting potentially dangerous, mosquito-borne viruses before they spread to people. Though 2026 has been the 15th driest year in Central Florida since record-keeping began over a century ago, regular and sometimes heavy afternoon downpours this month have provided good conditions for Aedes aegypti. “Small containers — their breeding habitats — are filled nearly daily with rainwater, and that’s a problem,” Harrison said. He said mosquito control follows the guidance of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, focusing their initial response within about 200 yards of the area of concern. “Our crews inspect properties yard-to-yard for mosquito breeding sites, particularly containers and other sources of standing water where Aedes aegypti mosquitoes can develop, and treat those sites as necessary,” he said. County crews also apply “larvicide treatments” using truck-mounted air-blast equipment. “These treatments are designed to reach water-holding containers and other mosquito-breeding habitats throughout the surrounding community and control mosquitoes while they are still in the larval stage,” Harrison said. Orange County Mosquito Control recently added new technology to its laboratory, allowing the agency to detect mosquito-borne illnesses, like dengue fever, more rapidly. The new molecular testing uses technology to look for genetic material of specific viruses within mosquito samples. Previously, samples were sent to outside laboratories. Specialist Rafael Melendez studies dead mosquitos to be tested for Dengue fever in the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Harrison said the county can now get same-day results, which lead to faster responses and mitigation efforts. As many as 111 people as of early September have contracted locally acquired dengue in six Florida counties this year, according to state data. While eight of these cases were in Miami-Dade and Palm Beach counties, a striking 95 occurred in Hillsborough County, where mosquito control teams are working overtime and ramping up spraying. The death of an 80-year-old South Tampa woman may be linked to a dengue infection. Frequent global travel significantly drives case numbers. So far this year, about 160 Floridians contracted dengue after traveling to endemic areas — most frequently Cuba. Mosquito experts point to hotter summers and increased rainfall as additional contributing factors. A common dengue symptom is a sudden high fever starting four to 10 days after a bite, followed by a skin rash a few days later. Treatment is limited to rest, fluids, and pain relievers. “There is no cure or antiviral medications for dengue,” said Dr. Rana Chakraborty, division chief in Pediatric Infectious Diseases at the University of Miami. Many infected individuals remain completely unaware. “A lot of people can get bitten, acquire dengue, and nothing happens to them,” Chakraborty said. “Only a fraction have symptoms.” For about 1 in 20 people, dengue progresses to a severe level — triggering repeated vomiting, nosebleeds, stomach pain, and organ failure — often requiring hospitalization. shudak@orlandosentinel.com

152 local cases in Florida By Josh Frigerio FOX 35 Orlando Orange County News Published September 18, 2026 12:51 PM EDT Share Copy Link Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Reddit Published September 18, 2026 12:51 PM EDT Orange County confirms 2 new locally acquired dengue cases Orange County health officials have confirmed two new locally acquired cases of dengue fever in Apopka, bringing the county's total to three cases and prompting a mosquito-borne illness alert. The Brief There have been 3 locally-acquired cases of dengue fever in Orange County, according to the Florida Department of Health. The two most recent cases were acquired in the Apopka area There have been more than 150 local cases of dengue reported in Florida, and 186 cases of international travel-related cases. ORANGE COUNTY, Fla. - There have been two more locally-acquired cases of dengue fever reported in Orange County, bringing the county total for the year to three, according to the Florida Department of Health and the Orange County Mosquito Control. County officials have now issued a mosquito alert and plan to target more areas with mosquito spray to reduce mosquito populations. New dengue cases reported in Orange County What we know: Officials said the two most recent cases were acquired in the Apopka area. What we don't know: Officials did not release specifics on the individuals who acquired the illness. More targeting mosquito spraying in Orange County What they're saying: "We are conducting targeted control measures and enhanced surveillance in Pine Hills, Apopka, and throughout Orange County," said Steve Harrison, manager of Orange County Mosquito Control. "While CDC guidance calls for targeted treatment of areas of concern, we are taking additional measures. Given the increased Dengue Fever cases we are seeing in other parts of Florida, we want to be proactive to reduce the risk of further local transmission in Orange County." By the numbers: According to the Florida Department of Health's latest arbovirus surveillance weekly report, which runs Sept. 6-12: 41 new cases of locally-acquired dengue in Florida; 152 cases reported year to date 26 new cases of international travel-related cases of dengue; 186 cases reported year to date What is dengue? Dig deeper: Dengue is a virus spread through bites from two species of mosquitoes, Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, according to Florida health officials. Both are found in Florida. When someone is infected, it can lead to dengue fever, a sometimes painful, debilitating disease. While rare, if symptoms are left untreated, it can be deadly. Dengue fever symptoms Symptoms typically appear 3-14 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito, and usually last 4-7 days. Symptoms are similar to those of influenza and other viruses: Sudden fever Severe headache Eye pain Muscle and joint pain Bleeding Vomiting and diarrhea Can it be deadly? Dengue hemorrhagic fever, a more severe form of dengue, is rare, but can be deadly if not recognized and/or treated with supportive care, according to the Florida Department of Health's website. Treatment There is no treatment for dengue fever or dengue hemorrhagic fever. However, people should manage symptoms and complications. Tips for avoiding mosquito bites What you can do: There are a number of mosquito-borne illnesses found in Florida, including West Nile, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, as well as travel-related illnesses, like chikungunya fever, dengue fever, malaria, yellow fever, and Rift Valley fever. Health officials are urging residents to take steps to prevent mosquito bites: Use insect repellent on exposed skin or clothing Remove standing water to stop mosquitoes from breeding Keep doors, exterior windows closed The Source: This story uses information from news releases issued by both the Florida Department of Health in Orange County and Orange County Mosquito Control, as well as information on Dengue fever from DOH and the CDC. content: India’s first approved dengue vaccine QDENGA likely to hit private market in 2027 QDENGA has been approved in 43 countries since 2022, with more than 32 million doses distributed globally, according to Takeda. South First Desk Published Sep 18, 2026 | 8:48 PM ⚊ Updated Sep 18, 2026 | 8:48 PM India’s dengue burden has been growing, with cases increasing 11-fold over the past two decades. Make Us Your Preferred Source on Google Synopsis: India’s first approved dengue vaccine, QDENGA, is expected to enter the private market in the first half of 2027, with Dr Reddy’s Laboratories handling its promotion and distribution in partnership with Takeda. The vaccine was approved by the CDSCO in July 2026 for people aged 4 to 60 and is given in two doses three months apart, with the company reporting efficacy against all four dengue virus serotypes. India’s first approved dengue vaccine is set to enter the country’s private market in 2027, with Hyderabad-based Dr Reddy’s Laboratories partnering with Japanese pharmaceutical company Takeda to promote and distribute its dengue vaccine QDENGA. It is expected to become available in the first half of 2027, subject to the completion of applicable regulatory processes. Dr Reddy’s will handle promotion and distribution in the private market, while Takeda will retain legal ownership and the rights to promote and distribute the vaccine in India’s public market. India’s dengue burden has been growing, with cases increasing 11-fold over the past two decades. A nationwide dengue surveillance study conducted by the Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratory network of the Indian Council of Medical Research found that all four dengue virus serotypes, DENV-1 to DENV-4, are circulating across multiple regions of India. The study also found that around one in 14 patients had a concurrent infection with multiple dengue serotypes. Also Read: Emergency contraceptive pills may soon carry new warnings on packs in India Approved in 43 countries QDENGA became India’s first CDSCO-approved dengue vaccine after receiving marketing authorisation from the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) in July 2026 for individuals aged 4 to 60 years. Also known as TAK-003, it is a live-attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccine designed to provide immune coverage against all four dengue virus serotypes. The vaccine is built on a DENV-2 backbone and contains structural proteins from DENV-1, DENV-3 and DENV-4. It is administered in two doses, three months apart. Takeda said its global clinical programme involved more than 60,000 participants across eight dengue-endemic countries. Its seven-year Phase 3 TIDES trial reported efficacy across all four dengue serotypes through seven years. QDENGA has been approved in 43 countries since 2022, with more than 32 million doses distributed globally, according to Takeda. The WHO has recommended the vaccine without pre-vaccination screening for use in high-endemic countries, and it has included the vaccine in its List of Prequalified Vaccines. content: Dr Reddy's, Takeda Ink Deal to Launch Dengue Vaccine QDENGA in India's Private Market in 2027 Hyderabad: Dr Reddy's Laboratories and Takeda Pharmaceutical Company have entered into an exclusive collaboration to promote and distribute QDENGA, Takeda's dengue vaccine, in India's private healthcare market. The partnership will cover both paediatric and adult vaccination. Subject to the completion of applicable processes with local authorities, the vaccine is expected to become available in India during the first half of 2027. QDENGA received marketing authorisation from the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) in July 2026 for use in individuals aged four to 60 years. According to the companies, it is the first dengue vaccine to receive approval in India. Under the agreement, Dr Reddy’s will be exclusively responsible for promoting, marketing and distributing QDENGA in India’s private market. Takeda will retain the rights to commercialise the vaccine in the country’s public market and will remain responsible for its manufacture and import. Takeda will also retain legal ownership of the vaccine and continue to oversee its medical, regulatory and brand strategy in India. The agreement does not involve any upfront consideration or milestone payments, while the remaining commercial terms have been kept confidential. The two companies will jointly support disease awareness, engagement with healthcare professionals and the private-market introduction of the vaccine in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements. Also Read: USFDA Issues Two Observations After Records Assessment of Dr. Reddy's Mexico API Facility The collaboration comes amid continuing concern over India’s dengue burden. According to information shared by the companies, reported dengue cases in the country have increased substantially over the past two decades. Surveillance findings have also shown that all four dengue virus serotypes—DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4—are circulating across multiple regions. M.V. Ramana, CEO, Global Generics, Dr Reddy’s Laboratories, described the approval of India’s first dengue vaccine as an important development for the country’s healthcare landscape. “Through our collaboration with Takeda, we look forward to making QDENGA available to eligible individuals and contributing to efforts aimed at addressing the country’s dengue burden,” he said. Dr Mahender Nayak, Head of Intercontinental Markets, International Business Unit, Takeda, said the company remained committed to supporting India’s evolving healthcare needs and expanding access to dengue vaccination. He also referred to the Parliamentary Committee on Health’s recommendation that a dengue vaccine be considered for inclusion in the Universal Immunisation Programme. In the meantime, the partnership with Dr Reddy’s is expected to facilitate access through the private market once QDENGA becomes commercially available. QDENGA, also known as TAK-003, is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine designed to provide protection against all four dengue virus serotypes. It is administered as a two-dose regimen, with the doses given three months apart. The vaccine has been evaluated through a global clinical programme involving more than 60,000 participants. This included the seven-year Phase III TIDES trial conducted across eight dengue-endemic countries. Since 2022, QDENGA has been approved in 43 countries, including India. More than 32 million doses have reportedly been distributed through public and private vaccination programmes worldwide. The vaccine has also been prequalified by the World Health Organization. Dr Reddy’s said the partnership supports its strategy to strengthen its vaccine business in India while contributing to wider public-health efforts aimed at reducing the country’s dengue burden. content: The Chenab Times Tamil Nadu Records Significant Spike in Dengue Cases: New Figures Revealed News Desk CT 2 days ago Aedes mosquito and a colorized transmission electron micrograph of dengue virus particles (yellow/r... — NIAID / CC BY 2.0 Ad New figures released by the Tamil Nadu State Health Department indicate a substantial increase in dengue cases over the past three years, prompting renewed attention to public health monitoring and vector control measures. The Chenab Times has learned that the latest data reveals a stark upward trend, with reported cases significantly exceeding previous estimates. The department’s figures show 56,863 dengue cases in 2023, followed by 46,971 cases in 2024. Projections for 2025 indicate a continued high incidence, with 25,585 cases already reported. These numbers represent a considerable deviation from the corresponding figures that were previously made available by the National Centre for Vector Borne Disease Control (NCVBDC). The discrepancy suggests a potential underestimation of the dengue burden in the state by national surveillance systems or a recent acceleration in case detection and reporting by the state health authorities. Health officials are reportedly reviewing the methodologies and data collection processes to understand the reasons behind this divergence. Dengue fever, a mosquito-borne viral infection, poses a significant public health challenge globally, and particularly in tropical and subtropical regions like Tamil Nadu. The disease can range in severity from mild febrile illness to severe dengue, which can be fatal. Common symptoms include high fever, severe headache, muscle and joint pain, rash, and nausea. The alarming rise in dengue cases underscores the persistent threat of vector-borne diseases and the critical need for robust public health infrastructure and community engagement. Factors contributing to the spread of dengue often include inadequate sanitation, poor waste management leading to breeding sites for mosquitoes, and climatic conditions that favour mosquito proliferation. Health experts emphasize that proactive measures are crucial in combating dengue outbreaks. These include source reduction of mosquito breeding sites through environmental management, personal protection against mosquito bites, and prompt diagnosis and treatment of infected individuals. Public awareness campaigns play a vital role in educating communities about preventive strategies and recognizing early symptoms of the disease. In response to the escalating figures, state health authorities are expected to intensify their surveillance activities, enhance public awareness programs, and reinforce vector control operations across the state. This includes increased fogging, larvicidal treatments, and promoting community participation in eliminating mosquito breeding grounds in and around residential areas. The release of these revised figures is anticipated to spur further investigation into the epidemiological patterns of dengue in Tamil Nadu and potentially influence policy decisions related to disease prevention and control at both state and national levels. The focus remains on mitigating the impact of the disease and protecting public health. News Desk CT The Chenab Times News Desk Exit mobile version

content: Play Now Log InSign Up Florida News Listen Live National News Weird News Local Traffic Local Weather Get News Alerts Florida News Hillsborough Dengue Cases Reach 134 as Florida Total Hits 152 By Rob Garguilo Sep 18, 2026 Photo: martinatobolova / iStock / Getty Images Hillsborough County, FL - Florida health officials reported another increase in locally acquired dengue infections, with Hillsborough County accounting for most of the state’s cases. The county has recorded 134 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, according to the latest Florida Department of Health arbovirus surveillance data. Florida’s statewide total has reached 152 cases. Locally acquired cases involve people infected by mosquitoes in Florida rather than during travel to another country or region where dengue circulates. Hillsborough previously reported 95 local infections through Sept. 5. The latest update added 39 cases to the county’s annual total. The infections have primarily involved dengue virus type 2, also known as DENV-2. State surveillance previously detected the same virus type in Aedes aegypti mosquito samples collected in Hillsborough County. Aedes aegypti mosquitoes commonly live near homes, bite during daylight hours and reproduce in containers holding standing water. Mosquitoes can acquire dengue by biting an infected person and later transmit the virus through additional bites. Dengue does not normally spread directly between people. Symptoms can include fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, nausea, vomiting, rash and muscle or joint pain. Most patients recover within about a week, but some develop severe dengue requiring immediate medical treatment. Warning signs may include intense abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, extreme fatigue, restlessness or difficulty breathing. Health officials recommend using insect repellent, wearing clothing that covers exposed skin, maintaining window and door screens, and removing standing water from buckets, flowerpots, tires, toys and other outdoor containers. Anyone experiencing possible dengue symptoms should contact a health care provider. Immediate treatment is recommended if severe warning signs develop. content: Dengue, spread by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, remains a serious health threat. Early consultation and prevention are key. AI Text size BALER, Aurora — Dengue cases in Aurora surged 137 percent from the same period last year, reaching 2,172 cases from 4 January to 12 September 2026, with seven deaths recorded, according to the Provincial Health Office. Children ages 1 to 10 accounted for nearly half of all infections, with 917 cases, or 42 percent of the provincial total. During the latest surveillance week, from 6 to 12 September, the PHO recorded 106 new cases. Patients ranged in age from 1 month to 104 years, with a median age of 12. Males accounted for half of all reported cases. Maria Aurora recorded the highest cumulative number of infections with 463 cases, followed by Dilasag with 413 and Dingalan with 394. Among newly reported cases, San Luis recorded the most with 32, followed by Maria Aurora with 26 and Dilasag with 21. Baler logged 11 new infections for a total of 242 cases, while Casiguran recorded eight new cases for a total of 253. Dipaculao and Dinalungan each reported one new case, bringing their totals to 69 and 37, respectively. Dilasag posted the province’s highest attack rate at 23.2 cases per 1,000 population, indicating a more intense concentration of infections compared with other municipalities. The PHO also reported clustering of dengue cases in 61 barangays across Aurora, showing that transmission was not confined to a single municipality. Nationwide, the Department of Health recorded 155,918 dengue cases, down 33 percent from the same period last year. Central Luzon, which includes Aurora, had the highest number of cases among the country’s regions with 21,242, followed by Calabarzon and Metro Manila. Health authorities have warned that rainy conditions and flooding create additional breeding grounds for mosquitoes that transmit dengue. Dengue can become life-threatening if severe symptoms are not recognized and treated promptly. Symptoms may include fever, severe headache, muscle and joint pain, vomiting and rashes. Provincial health officials urged households to eliminate mosquito breeding sites, use protective measures such as mosquito nets and repellents, seek immediate medical consultation when symptoms develop and support targeted fogging in outbreak areas. “Dengue prevention is everyone’s responsibility. Act now, clean your surroundings, and help us stop this outbreak,” the PHO said. Authorities stressed that early detection and prompt medical attention remain critical in preventing severe dengue as rains continue across the province

content: Homepage Latest News Cuba News Miami News Blackouts today Informal Exchange Rate Videos Entertainment Sports International News Opinion CiberCuba Interviews United States Cuisine Florida Spain Culture Motor Readings Tourism History Nature Health Close the sidebar ESENFRIT Florida is facing a severe dengue outbreak and has confirmed its first death of the year Latest News By CiberCuba Editorial Team Monday, September 21, 2026 - 12:36 Aedes aegypti (Reference image)Photo © Wikimedia Commons Florida confirmed its first death from dengue in 2026 amid a rise in infections acquired within the state, with Hillsborough County in the Tampa area becoming the main hotspot of the outbreak. The Florida Department of Health confirmed the death on Friday, according to AP, while local reports indicated that the victim was an 80-year-old woman from Tampa who died on September 4. The confirmation comes when the official data itself shows an unusual expansion of transmission. The latest arbovirus surveillance report from the Florida Department of Health, corresponding to the week of September 6 to 12, recorded 152 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, spread across six counties. The vast majority are concentrated in Hillsborough, with 134 local infections, followed by Miami-Dade and Pinellas, with seven cases each; Pasco, with two; and Orange and Palm Beach, with one each in that official count. The growth has been particularly rapid in Hillsborough. On September 4, Florida's Surgeon General, Joseph Ladapo, officially reported 59 locally acquired infections in that county. Just over a week later, the state report recorded 134. Furthermore, the Orange County Health Department announced last Friday two additional local cases of dengue, subsequent to the period covered by the latest available weekly report, so the state count will continue to be adjusted as new reports come in. Florida is experiencing one of its most intense years of local transmission in recent times. According to the historical statistics from the Florida Department of Health, in 2023 the state recorded 199 locally acquired dengue cases, the highest number in the published series for the period 2014-2024. Dengue is a viral disease primarily transmitted through the bite of the Aedes aegypti mosquito. It can cause fever, severe muscle and joint pain, headache, and skin rashes; in severe cases, it may lead to bleeding, shock, and even death. Authorities have intensified surveillance and mosquito control in the affected areas. The Department of Health recommends using repellents registered with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), wearing clothing that covers arms and legs when possible, and eliminating any standing water around homes and businesses, as even small amounts can become breeding grounds. The increase is not limited to Tampa Bay. Miami-Dade confirmed a locally acquired case of dengue in early August, while other counties were later added to the list of areas with local transmission. At the beginning of September, dengue cases were already showing a significant increase in Florida, with local transmission hotspots in various areas of the southern and central parts of the state. Health Dengue fever cases rise in Florida, with 3 new cases in Lee County and a death in Hillsborough County WGCU | By Cary Barbor, Jennifer Crawford Published September 21, 2026 at 10:26 AM EDT Facebook LinkedIn Email Print Three new cases of Dengue fever in Lee County and a death from the disease in Hillsborough County are part of the reported rise in cases of the mosquito-spread virus in Florida. Cases of the disease in the U.S. are typically picked up elsewhere in the world and brought home by travelers. That is the situation with the three cases in Lee County according to Jennifer McBride, Lee County Mosquito Control public information officer. McBride said those in Lee County who acquired the disease contracted it in Cuba and that there have been no locally-obtained dengue cases. "It starts with an international case," she said. "We have people travel somewhere, they've been bitten by a mosquito that's infected with dengue. They come back. The thing about dengue is about 80% of patients actually are asymptomatic. They don't have symptoms, which could be a problem. So they come back to here and a mosquito will bite them. It becomes infected with the dengue and then it will bite someone that has not traveled and it becomes localized. And very quickly then that takes off. So those mosquitoes are then transmitting a local case of dengue." Support for WGCU Provided By: U.S. Centers for Disease Control In the United States, there have been nearly 1,500 locally acquired U.S. cases, most of them in Puerto Rico, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Florida’s largest number — nearly 200 — was reported in 2023. This year, Florida alone reported 152 locally acquired cases of the disease, meaning it was spread by mosquito bites in the state. 134 of the cases are in Hillsborough County. Dengue can cause a high fever, joint pain and headache. The current outbreak is centered just north of Tampa, and workers have been spraying to kill mosquitoes day and night. They also have been checking properties for pooled water, including in tires, where mosquitoes might breed, said Paolo Pecora, senior environmental scientist for Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services. The CDC shows that more than 330 cases have been reported in Florida in 2026 with eight cases in Lee County. McBride said that many of the cases reported in Hillsborough have also been linked to being acquired in Cuba. For now, McBride said, Lee County Mosquito Control personnel have been going door-to-door in Lee County requesting access to backyards and other areas to look for possible breeding sites for mosquitoes such as standing water in containers. The type of mosquito linked to the dengue cases is what's identified as the "backyard mosquito" also known as aedes aegypti. Another viral disease spread by mosquitoes is chikungunya. In the week ended September 12, eight new cases were reported in Miami-Dade county. This illness also is characterized by a high fever and joint pain. Support for WGCU Provided By: The best way to avoid transmission is to avoid mosquito bites. Drain standing water from around your home, wear long sleeves and pants outdoors when possible, and protect yourself with mosquito repellant. Dengue at a glance/CDC data All four dengue viruses are spread to people primarily through the bite of an infected Aedes species mosquito. Protect yourself from dengue by avoiding mosquito bites. There are no dengue vaccines currently available in the United States. Prevention The best way to prevent dengue is to protect yourself from mosquito bites. Use insect repellent. Wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and pants. Take steps to control mosquitoes in and around your home. If you think you have dengue See a healthcare provider if you develop a fever or have symptoms of dengue. Tell him or her about any recent travel. Rest as much as possible. Take acetaminophen (also known as paracetamol outside of the US) to control fever and relieve pain — Do not take aspirin or ibuprofen! Drink plenty of fluids to stay hydrated. Drink water or drinks with added electrolytes. For mild symptoms, care for a sick infant, child, or family member at home. Important tip If you have dengue, prevent mosquito bites. During the first week of illness, dengue can be found in the blood. The virus can be passed from an infected person to a mosquito through mosquito bites. Thank you. The Associated Press contributed to this report. FOX 13's Ariel Plasencia reports. The Brief Hillsborough County now accounts for 88% of Florida’s locally acquired dengue cases, with 134 infections reported so far, according to recent state health data. Doctors with Tampa General Hospital estimate they’ve treated over 100 dengue patients, and symptoms include a "break-bone fever." Mosquito control crews are deploying helicopters and trucks in an aggressive campaign to kill mosquito larvae, as well as adult mosquitos. TAMPA, Fla. - More than 130 cases of dengue have been reported in Hillsborough County, making up 88% of the state’s total infections, according to most recent data from Florida health officials. Of those, the Florida Department of Health also confirmed the first dengue fever-related death in the county. The numbers show 39 cases of dengue were reported in Hillsborough County from Sept. 6-12 alone. Meanwhile, seven total cases have been reported in Pinellas County and Pasco County has two cases. The treatment plan Local perspective: Crews with Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services will continue to use helicopters and trucks to spray treatment, aimed at killing both adult mosquitos and mosquito larvae. County officials told FOX 13 they believe these efforts appear to be working because mosquito trap numbers are dropping in certain locations. Additionally, samples of adult mosquitos from local traps have come back negative for dengue over the last two weeks. Furthermore, laboratory testing confirms that potentially infected female mosquitoes are not passing the virus down to their offspring, Hillsborough County Mosquito Management officials said. "It makes me feel good. Again, it's a suppression and eradication campaign," Paolo Pecora, Hillsborough County Mosquito Management senior environmental scientist, told FOX 13. "We want to go into there and make sure that we are eliminating any flying disease vector that can potentially transmit this virus to our residents." Why you should care: But, they aren’t letting their guard down. County officials don’t want mosquitos that have already bitten somebody with dengue to go and bite somebody else, resulting in more human cases. So, they’re asking for the public’s help. "This mosquito species is strictly containers. Not ditches, not sewer drainage areas, not lakes and ponds. It's containers," said Pecora. "They are utilizing and have evolved with mankind through civilizations to utilize man-made objects. That’s why this is such a challenge and why we’re asking our residents to come out and help us." What you can do: Residents are urged to dump any standing water on their property and to wear bug spray when spending time outdoors. Local doctors treating dengue What they're saying: Doctors with Tampa General Hospital estimate they’ve treated more than 100 dengue patients, telling FOX 13 one of the common symptoms is a "break-bone fever." "The body aches are so intense that it's got this nickname as 'break-bone fever,'" said Dr. Kartik Cherabuddi, the chief hospital epidemiology officer at Tampa General Hospital. "It's real, and I've seen patients — they hurt so bad, it's the predominant thing that’s bringing them into the emergency room." Along with severe joint, bone, and muscle pain, common symptoms include nausea and pain behind the eyes. "It's the time the fever breaks. The next two days is when you can have more severe warning signs. If you have severe abdominal pain, persistently throwing up, bleeding from the gums or other sites, difficulty breathing — and critically, that’s when the fever starts to go down is when these could develop," Cherabuddi added. "That's when you absolutely have to go to the ER." He said one in four who are infected will develop the illness — and roughly one in 20 symptomatic people developed more severe disease. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from the Florida Department of Health, who provided recent infection data, as well as officials from Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services and doctors at Tampa General Hospital. Bridges USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Sept. 18, 2026, 12:59 p.m. ET Florida is experiencing a surge in locally acquired dengue fever cases, with 152 reported as of mid-September. The vast majority of cases, 134 in total, have been confirmed in Hillsborough County. Dengue is a mosquito-borne illness with symptoms including fever, severe pain, and rash. Florida is experiencing a surge in dengue fever, a mosquito-borne illness that causes aches, pains, nausea, vomiting, and rash, according to state health data. The state reported 41 new locally acquired cases — meaning that people caught it in Florida, not while traveling abroad — in just the last week, bring the state total to 152 as of Sept. 12. Last year, 62 people tested positive. Nearly all of the cases have been reported in one area: Hillsborough County, home of Tampa, which has reported 134 confirmed locally acquired cases. The other 18 cases have been reported in Miami-Dade, Pinellas, Pasco, Orange, and Palm Beach counties. There have also been 186 dengue cases acquired this year from international travel. Shop mosquito repellent at Amazon Currently, 11 counties are under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites. Other mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida Health officials track several different endemic mosquito-borne viruses such as West Nile virus, Eastern equine encephalitis virus (EEEV), St. Louis encephalitis virus, chikungunya virus, Zika virus (ZIKV), malaria, and California encephalitis group viruses. As of Sept. 12, five cases of West Nile virus have been reported in Florida, two of them asymptomatic, although the illness has been rapidly rising on the U.S. West Coast. One case of locally acquired and 66 cases of travel-based chikungunya fever also have been reported. Where has dengue been reported in Florida? According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Sept. 17, there have been 152 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported, which is up from 111 reported on Sept. 5. Hillsborough County: 134 (which jumped from 95 the week before) Miami-Dade County: 7 Pinellas County: 7 Pasco County: 2 Orange County: 1 Palm Beach County: 1 What is dengue fever? What are the symptoms? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include a sudden onset of fever, severe headaches, eye pain, muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”), bleeding, and in some cases, gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea. Dengue is spread by mosquitoes that bite people who have the virus and spread it to others. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue can be caused by one of four related viruses: dengue virus 1, 2, 3, and 4. The bulk of the detected cases in Florida have been DENV-2. What is Florida doing to prevent dengue infections? The Florida Department Health has advised residents to take precautions against mosquito bites. “Use insect repellent, cover up when possible, and remove standing water around your home. Individual prevention helps protect you and your community,” State Surgeon General Dr. Joseph A. Ladapo said in a release. Affected counties have increased mosquito spraying and tested for dengue in mosquito pools to track the spread. So far, 16 DENV-2-infected mosquito pools have been found in Hillsborough County, according to health department data. How to avoid dengue fever The best way is to avoid getting bitten by mosquitos, especially if you live in an area under a mosquito alert or advisory. According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. C. A. content: Gulfport leaders brought residents and mosquito-control officials together Monday night to answer questions about dengue as locally acquired cases continue to be reported across Tampa Bay. Vice Mayor Marlene Shaw said she organized the town hall after hearing misinformation and concerns about the virus and Pinellas County's mosquito-control response. "There has been so much conversation going on. I refer to it as chatter because a lot of it is misinformed information," Shaw said. "They're just going off in all different directions rather than going right to the facts." Shaw said she also had questions about mosquito-control treatments, including whether they could affect pollinators or be applied on private property. "There were so many reasons that even I was concerned," she said. Pinellas County is using Bti, or Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis , to target mosquito larvae in standing water before they develop into biting adults. The naturally occurring soil bacterium produces toxins that target the larvae of mosquitoes, blackflies and fungus gnats, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. The EPA says Bti does not pose a risk to people. Caroline Pickart, a senior environmental specialist with Pinellas County Mosquito Control, also addressed misconceptions about when dengue-carrying mosquitoes are active. The two primary mosquito species capable of spreading dengue, Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus , are daytime biters. An infected mosquito can transmit the virus through a single bite. "If a mosquito is infected with dengue, it does have the ability to pass that on to us when it bites us," Pickart said. "And that's through the ability of when they are biting us, they actually spit inside of us." Florida Department of Health data show 152 locally acquired dengue cases statewide through Sept. 12. That includes 134 cases linked to exposure in Hillsborough County, seven in Pinellas County and two in Pasco County. Warning signs can emerge within 24 to 48 hours after a fever goes away and may include abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding or extreme fatigue and restlessness. The Florida Department of Health confirmed the death in a statement shared with USA TODAY on Friday, Sept. 18, which it says occurred in Hillsborough County. The state's health department reported on Sept. 12 that it had 153 locally acquired cases, meaning people caught it in Florida, not while traveling abroad. About 1 in 20 people who contract dengue develop a more serious illness called hemorrhagic fever, according to the CDC, which can entail symptoms like abdominal pain, frequent vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums and blood in stool or vomit. This season has been particularly active for mosquito-borne illnesses nationwide, especially West Nile and dengue. Bridges Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Updated Sept. 21, 2026, 2:11 p.m. ET Florida has reported its first dengue fever death of 2026 amid a surge in mosquito-borne illnesses. The death occurred in Hillsborough County, the hotspot for locally acquired cases in the state. State officials have reported 338 total dengue cases this year, with 152 acquired locally. Florida has reported the first dengue fever death of 2026 as cases of mosquito-borne illnesses surge in the state. The death occurred in Hillsborough County, the hotspot of this year's dengue cases, according to a statement from the Florida Department of Health shared with USA TODAY on Friday, Sept. 18. "We are reminding all residents and visitors throughout the state to take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying insect repellent, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, draining any standing water, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible – especially during sunrise and sunset, when mosquitoes are most active," spokesperson Claire Maher said in a statement. The Tampa Bay Times was the first to report on the death, which it says occurred at Tampa General Hospital. The victim was 80-year-old Gay Small, the outlet reported. She died of “dengue infection” along with “septic shock” and “multi-organ failure," according to a death certificate obtained by the Times. How many 2026 dengue cases in Florida Florida officials have reported 338 cases of dengue fever this year as of Sept. 12, with 152 case acquired within the state and the rest from international travel. Of those local cases, 134 were reported in Hillsborough County. The other 18 cases have been reported in Miami-Dade, Pinellas, Pasco, Orange, and Palm Beach counties. That's a 145% increase in locally acquired cases over 2025, which saw 62. As of Sept. 17, 11 counties were under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. What is dengue fever? What are the symptoms? According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, dengue symptoms are very flu-like and include aches and pains, nausea, vomiting, and rash. About 1 in 20 people who contract dengue develop a more serious illness called hemorrhagic fever, which can bring symptoms like abdominal pain, frequent vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, and blood in stool or vomit. "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito. Where has dengue been reported in Florida? According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Sept. 17, Florida had reported 152 locally acquired dengue cases, up from 111 reported on Sept. 5. Hillsborough County: 134 (which jumped from 95 the week before) Miami-Dade County: 7 Pinellas County: 7 Pasco County: 2 Orange County: 1 Palm Beach County: 1 Which Florida counties are at risk for dengue fever? A mosquito-borne illness advisory (meaning residents should avoid mosquito bites) has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Brevard Leon Orange Palm Beach Pasco Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert (meaning there has been a rise in disease activity and residents should take extra precautions) has been issued for the following counties: Duval Hillsborough Miami-Dade Pinellas What is Florida doing to prevent dengue infections? The Florida Department of Health has advised residents to take precautions against mosquito bites. “Use insect repellent, cover up when possible, and remove standing water around your home. Individual prevention helps protect you and your community,” State Surgeon General Dr. Joseph A. Ladapo said in a release. Affected counties have increased mosquito spraying. So far, health department data show 16 DENV-2-infected mosquito pools in Hillsborough County. How to avoid dengue fever The best way is to avoid mosquito bites, especially if you live in an area under a mosquito alert or advisory. According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. C. A.
